artboards.title: 11 · Expanded — what I tried, and what you can do
12 · Get help — a handoff, not the founder's problem

annotations.text:
Two panes, fixed.

Left: the conversation — what you asked, what's happening. Ephemeral.

Right: Your product — the durable list of what exists, always visible, never pushed off screen by chat. Each row expands in place.

The sidebar is the answer to "what do I have?" and it should never require scrolling the chat to see.

Screen 3 is the gate that stops the agent silently building more than was asked.

Unchecking "a place to store photos" auto-unchecks "something to resize them", with the line: this needs somewhere to put the photos first.

The founder can't judge infrastructure, but they can judge "I never asked for email."

The design argument lives in screens 4-7.

There is deliberately NO status meaning "started but unverified" — something created but unproven stays "setting up…". It never gets to look like success.

That missing state is why the verification gate can't be quietly downgraded later: there is nowhere in the UI to put a half-truth.

No celebration on success — no banner, no "All set!". Something working is the expected outcome, not an achievement. This is the design's most likely point of failure: resist the instinct to reward the user.

Same restraint on the other side: no red, no warning triangles. A failure is stated, not alarmed about.

Row 10-12 is the disclosure rule, corrected.

"No jargon" and "no depth" are different rules. A doctor's report has depth — a summary line, then what was measured, then what to do. The register stays plain; the detail doesn't disappear.

So: expanding a row reveals MORE PLAIN LANGUAGE, never more jargon.

Screen 12 is where the event contract's `dev` channel finally surfaces — real service names, commands, exit codes.

The jargon rule survives because this panel is explicitly ADDRESSED TO SOMEONE ELSE. It isn't the founder failing to understand; it's a handoff, labelled as one.

The honest answer to "how does a founder debug?" is: they don't, they forward.

One Floci instance holds many products side by side — they only collide if they pick the same resource names, and the catalog generates those.

So the switcher is a header, not a sidebar: a founder has products, not sessions.

Cheap to build toward now (prefix resource names, key state by product). The switcher UI itself is deferrable — it shouldn't compete with the verification gate.

Screen 8 has a second variant, for when nothing in the catalog is close enough to offer:

"I can't set that up yet — it's not something I know how to do properly, and I'd rather say so than get it wrong. I've made a note of what you asked for."

This should read as competence, not limitation.

Export is the answer to "what does the founder walk away with?"

Same two-audience split as everything else: the plain page (15) is what a founder sends an investor or cofounder — their own words, their own diagram. The technical one (16) is what a developer picks up.

One checkbox in the dialog switches between them: "Technical details — for a developer". Off by default.

The diagram is the part worth building even if the rest slips: it's the only view that shows how the pieces connect.
